headline: Washington as Shareholder: The U.S. Government's $21 Billion Industrial Equity Portfolio
lede: Over the past year, the federal government has quietly become a direct equity investor in semiconductors and rare-earth mining — a novel experiment in industrial policy that borrows the logic of Singapore's Temasek while lacking its institutional insulation from political interference.
body:
The United States government does not, in the conventional sense, own stocks. That changed in 2025. Through a sequence of deals spanning the CHIPS and Science Act, the Defense Production Act, and Department of Energy loan conversions, the Trump administration has assembled direct equity stakes in at least eleven companies, with committed capital exceeding ten billion dollars and paper gains that, on some accounts, have already dwarfed the original outlay.

The largest position is in Intel. In August 2025 the Commerce Department converted $5.7 billion in unspent CHIPS Act grants — originally structured as subsidies — and $3.2 billion from the Secure Enclave program into 433.3 million primary shares of Intel common stock at $20.47 per share, equivalent to a 9.9% stake. The government also received a five-year warrant covering an additional 5%. Intel shares, which languished below $25 for most of 2024 amid foundry losses, surged through 2025 on restructuring news and AI-adjacent chip demand; by late April 2026 they were trading above $95. The unrealized gain on the common position alone exceeds $30 billion — a figure that makes the $11.6B claim in the viral post look conservative rather than inflated.

The rare-earth positions are smaller but strategically freighted. In July 2025 the Defense Department — which President Trump rebranded the Department of War — agreed to purchase $400 million of convertible preferred stock in MP Materials, the operator of Mountain Pass, California, the only producing rare-earth processing site in the United States. Exercising associated warrants would give the Pentagon a 15% stake, making it MP's largest single shareholder. The deal bundled a purchase agreement for 100% of output from a planned 10,000-metric-ton magnet plant and a price floor of $110 per kilogram for rare-earth compounds, effectively backstopping MP's economics against Chinese price suppression. MP shares gained roughly 224% in calendar 2025. In September 2025 the Defense Department paid $35.6 million for a 10% stake in Trilogy Metals, a pre-revenue explorer whose Upper Kobuk copper and cobalt projects sit in Alaska's Ambler Mining District; the stock spiked ninefold before retreating as permitting risk reasserted itself. In October, the Department of Energy converted part of a $2.23 billion construction loan to Lithium Americas into a 5% warrant-based stake in the Thacker Pass lithium project in Nevada, a joint venture with General Motors.

The 167% return and $21.48 billion portfolio value cited in the post appear to be a snapshot from a third-party tracking dashboard that aggregates the cost bases of disclosed positions against market prices at the time of capture. The figure is plausible for a measurement window that excludes the Intel position's most dramatic appreciation, which occurred largely in April 2026 — a single month in which INTC gained roughly 100%. As of early May 2026, the Intel stake alone is worth over $41 billion against an $8.9 billion outlay, making the portfolio's true unrealized gain substantially larger than $11.6 billion. The dashboard figures should therefore be read as a floor, not a ceiling, and the precise methodology — which positions are included, at what conversion ratios — matters enormously.

The precedent question is the one that will outlast any return figure. The United States has held crisis equity before: the Treasury's 2008 bank stakes under TARP (the Troubled Asset Relief Program, an emergency purchase of bank preferred shares after the financial crisis), and the 2009 GM and Chrysler bailouts. Both were presented as reluctant, temporary interventions. The current program differs in ambition: these are proactive industrial bets, not rescues, and the administration has shown no particular interest in exit timelines. Comparisons to Norway's Government Pension Fund Global (a state investment vehicle funded by oil revenues and required by law to invest entirely outside Norway) or Singapore's Temasek (a state holding company that manages former government enterprises) are structurally strained. Neither operates inside a separation-of-powers system where the regulator and the shareholder are the same entity. The CSIS has noted that a government simultaneously holding equity in Intel while setting semiconductor export policy, or in MP Materials while determining rare-earth tariff schedules, creates conflicts with no clean resolution. The moral hazard runs in both directions: companies with a government shareholder may take risks they would otherwise avoid, and governments with equity stakes may set policy to protect their book.

Whether this amounts to sovereign wealth management or to managed industrial patronage depends on a question the administration has not answered: what is the exit strategy? Norway's fund has one. Temasek has one. The Trump portfolio, as currently constructed, has a political logic — reduce Chinese supply-chain leverage — but no disclosed financial governance framework. Until that distinction is resolved, the impressive return figures are less a vindication of the strategy than a reason to ask harder questions about it.

concepts.definition: A state-owned investment vehicle that deploys government savings — typically from commodity revenues or trade surpluses — into diversified financial assets. Norway's Government Pension Fund Global and Singapore's Temasek are canonical examples. Distinguished from the current U.S. portfolio by having dedicated governance frameworks, explicit return mandates, and separation from the ministries that regulate the industries they invest in.

A group of 17 chemically similar metallic elements — including neodymium, praseodymium, and dysprosium — used in permanent magnets for electric motors, wind turbines, and missile guidance systems. China processes roughly 85–90% of the world's supply, giving it significant leverage over defense and clean-energy manufacturing elsewhere.

The Creating Helpful Incentives to Produce Semiconductors and Science Act, signed in August 2022, authorizing approximately $52 billion in federal subsidies to revive domestic semiconductor manufacturing and research. The Intel equity stake was formed by converting unspent CHIPS grant allocations into common shares rather than disbursing them as cash subsidies.

A 1950 U.S. law that grants the executive branch broad authority to direct industrial production to meet national defense requirements, including the ability to provide loans, purchase agreements, and — more recently — equity investments in companies deemed critical to the defense supply chain. Used to authorize the MP Materials and Trilogy Metals stakes.

fact_check: The 167% / $11.6B claim is plausible but appears to be a point-in-time snapshot that significantly understates the current portfolio performance. The Intel stake alone — purchased at $20.47/share in August 2025, trading above $95 by May 2026 — represents an unrealized gain exceeding $30 billion on the $8.9B outlay, roughly 3.5x the $11.6B figure cited. MP Materials gained ~224% in 2025; Trilogy Metals spiked sharply then partially reversed; Lithium Americas is up ~69% from its post-deal lows. The $21.48B total portfolio value in the dashboard OCR likely reflects a measurement date before Intel's April 2026 surge. The 167% return is directionally accurate for a subset of positions or an earlier snapshot, but the aggregate unrealized gain as of May 2026 is materially higher. The tweet does not distinguish between government-held equity (Intel, MP, TMQ, LAC) and the unrelated Trump-family crypto and media holdings (Truth Social / DJT, World Liberty Financial) — those are separate portfolios.
